description: Your child's doctor must be willing to testify to a “reasonable degree of medical certainty” that the trauma caused or will cause future deficits.
shortAnswer: Your child's doctor must be willing to testify to a “reasonable degree of medical certainty” that the trauma sustained by your child caused or will cause the future deficits. Many doctors are not aware of the correct legal standard. I talk with my client's doctors before they give any testimony and educate them on the correct standard of proof.

faq.q: Why is a child's head injury hard to prove in a legal claim?
faq.a: In children, some neurological deficits after head trauma may not manifest for many years. Injury to the frontal lobes may not become apparent until the child reaches adolescence, and injury to reading and writing centers may not become apparent until the child reaches school age.

faq.q: What does “a reasonable degree of medical certainty” mean?
faq.a: In actual trial practice the evidentiary standard is “more likely than not” or “more probable than not.” This is a lower standard of proof than certainty and also lower than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard.

faq.q: Why are some doctors reluctant to support a child's head injury claim?
faq.a: They don't want to get involved with a legal claim unless there is overwhelming proof that the trauma caused a deficit. They in effect think there must be enough evidence to prove it “beyond a reasonable doubt.” This results in many families not getting enough compensation to provide for the future care of their injured child.

faq.q: Can I reopen my child's head injury case if new deficits appear later?
faq.a: The law only allows the family “one bite of the apple”, one chance to get justice, and when the legal claim ends they can never reopen the case even if it turns out their child has far more profound deficits than we proved.
